data.title: Live updates: Trump briefs reporters on China summit; GOP at odds over reconciliation
data.description:
President Trump, fresh from his trip to Asia, is set to brief reporters on his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump touted the rare summit as “Great and Highly Consequential” in a post online following the meeting. Earlier Thursday, the trio announced the talks yielded a symbolic “declaration toward peace.”

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans are increasingly at odds over the Trump administration’s push for a $350 billion Pentagon funding package. Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) warned that the reconciliation process could expose deep divisions within the GOP over Medicaid cuts enacted last year.

Some lawmakers are eager to revisit the healthcare reductions, while others fear reopening the debate could unravel key provisions of Trump’s signature tax law. Hill Insiders can learn more here.

On Thursday, Senate Republicans blocked another war powers resolution that would restrict further military operations in Iran. The upper chamber did advance the bipartisan permitting reform bill though, sending it to the House.

A federal district court in Virginia will also hear arguments Friday on a lawsuit seeking to prevent the construction of Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch. The hearing comes two days after a federal judge extended the block on construction.

Trump will host a reception in the afternoon and hold signing time. First lady Melania Trump, whose docuseries premiered late Thursday on Prime Video, will attend an arrival ceremony for the White House Christmas tree.

Follow live below.

data.title: Democrats press Lutnick for Megaspeed investigation findings
data.description:
Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, are pressing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for information about the agency’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company, is facing a probe from the Department of Commerce and Department of Justice (DOJ) over whether it helped smuggle advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

But Commerce’s role in the investigation has come under scrutiny after The New York Times reported that Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter reached out to agents working on the case last year.

Teter reportedly said Under Secretary of Commerce Jeff Kessler had given the company permission to reach out. Kessler heads up the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which oversees export controls.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” Kamlager-Dove and Meeks wrote in a letter to Lutnick on Thursday.

The case was transferred to the DOJ shortly after Teter’s outreach, according to The Times. The agencies said in a joint statement Monday that the Justice Department “took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed” following an on-site inspection of the company last June.

The lawmakers called for answers as to “whether Under Secretary Kessler permitted or encouraged Nvidia to contact BIS agents actively investigating transactions in which the company was involved, and whether the Department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and personally linked to the Trump Administration to interfere with law enforcement activity.”

They are seeking information about when BIS launched its investigation into Megaspeed, what information was gathered, whether the probe was halted, what communications Kessler had with Nvidia about Megaspeed and whether Nvidia received any nonpublic information.

“The Department of Commerce has a responsibility to protect American national security, enforce export control laws, and ensure that no corporation receives preferential treatment in matters involving potential violations of federal law,” they added.

data.title: These 14 Democratic senators voted to loosen environmental laws to speed up energy buildout
data.description:
The Senate voted late Thursday night to pass a law that seeks to speed up the nation’s energy and infrastructure buildout, including by loosening its environmental laws.

The bill was a bipartisan push, spearheaded by Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (N.M.) alongside Republicans Shelley Moore Capito (W.Va.) and Mike Lee (Utah).

Nevertheless, most Democrats opposed the law, citing among their concerns its loosening of environmental laws, lessening of tribal input into projects that may impact them and potential to bolster fossil fuel production and infrastructure.

The bill particularly makes changes to the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act.

This includes language that makes it harder for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and states to block projects on environmental grounds.

It also includes language exempting certain activities, including expansions to natural gas pipelines; makes it more difficult for opponents of a project to sue over it; extends how long water quality permits can last before they need to be renewed; and adds hurdles to the EPA’s ability to set water quality criteria. 

It also changes the Endangered Species Act, including a change to the definition of “best available science” that’s required to be used to determine whether a species should get legal protections — in a way that environmentalists say creates a high threshold for protections. 

These fourteen Democrats voted for it: Whitehouse, Heinrich, Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (R.I.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.) and Mark Warner (Va.). Also among the yes votes was Angus King (I-Maine), who caucuses with Democrats.

The bill also contains significant wins for Democrats on climate and renewable energy — and the bill’s Democratic supporters point to analyses showing that it’s actually projected to bring down U.S. emissions.

Among the key provisions expected to bolster solar and wind power is a new authority granted to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission allowing it to approve new powerlines when states don’t do so, which is expected to help get more renewable power onto the grid. 

It also contains provisions that would force data centers to pay for any electricity cost increases their demand would cause. Supporters have pointed to one analysis saying the bill will save consumers $50 to $78 per year on their electric bills in 2040.

Whitehouse and Heinrich have been championing the legislation calling it a win for the climate as well as affordability. 

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” Heinrich said in a statement on the legislation. 

“This bill kicks off Democrats bringing down energy costs, lowering emissions, creating well-paying jobs, and ending the free ride for data centers,” Whitehouse said in his own statement. “Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit.”

Other Democratic and Democratic-caucusing supporters seemed torn. In a statement shared with The Hill, King said that his vote “wasn’t an easy choice.”

“I listened to my environmental friends in Maine, many of whom were opposed to the bill, I talked to people in the energy field, particularly in the renewable field, and decided that on balance this bill is a lot better than the status quo,” King said. 

“This bill unlocks an enormous amount of renewable energy, that is now basically unable to get to the market because of a lack of transmission,” he added.

data.title: Stock investors are giving up on China
data.description:
China’s closely watched CSI 300 Index has fallen 20 percent from June highs and is now officially in bear-market territory.  

Chinese stocks have lost more than $3.5 trillion in value since the middle of the year. Many analysts believe that shares are still on a downward path. Morgan Stanley, for instance, sees perhaps another 15 percent drop.

“If the country is winning the future, why are its investors so glum?” asks the Economist in an article titled “China’s Stock Markets Are the Great Global Exception.” The S&P 500 in the U.S. has gained 53 percent over the last five years. In Europe, the FTSE 500 has gained 45 percent. The CSI 300 has now lost 18.5 percent in the same period.

Chinese stocks are hitting lows for two fundamental reasons. For one thing, Xi Jinping’s economic plans are not working. Second, Xi is adopting policies that reduce or even eliminate profits at listed companies, scaring away investors — especially domestic investors.  

On the first point, the Chinese economy, especially from the outside, looks bright and shiny because of the country’s leadership in a number of crucial technology areas. Xi’s Made in China 2025 initiative and five-year plans — China is now in the first year of its 15th five-year plan — along with associated programs, are all tech-heavy.

“The country’s technology companies are forging ahead,” Andrew Collier, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Mossavar-Rahmani Center, told me this month. He noted that corporate profits for high technology manufacturing rose 52 percent in the first nine months of this year. However, such manufacturing only accounts for roughly 6 percent of the country’s economy.

Optimists point out that the export sector is another success story. The country’s trade surplus at the end of October hit a stunning $1.04 trillion. But paradoxically, many export-oriented factories are earning only thin margins and are not doing well. This appears to be the reason why the central government, through brazen currency interventions, is slowing the rise of the renminbi. The manipulation is of course attracting criticism from the country’s trading partners.

The rest of the economy is deteriorating fast. The property sector at the end of last decade accounted for about a quarter of gross domestic product. Now, the extreme oversupply — the country has more vacant housing than its entire population of 1.4 billion people could fill — is weighing heavily on growth.

With housing prices falling, a negative wealth effect is weighing on consumption. Furthermore, Xi’s relentless drive for automation, which is producing the world’s most advanced robots, is aggravating both unemployment and underemployment.

Urban unemployment, officially pegged at 5.2 percent in September, is probably closer to 20 percent overall and much higher for the crucial 16 to 24 age cohort. Some recent college graduates are not even looking for white-collar jobs, heading straight to menial employment out of school. Gig jobs employ a stunning 44 percent of the country’s workforce. 

Consumption in China accounts for only about 38 percent of GDP, one of the lowest consumption-contribution rates in the world. And from all indications consumption’s role is continuing to decline.

The central government has sporadically introduced measures to stimulate consumer spending, but they are almost always one-off programs that have no lasting effect. Xi has not implemented structural reforms that will empower consumers at the expense of state enterprises and state banks.

In sum, GDP growth, in reality, is almost certainly less than the 4.5 percent reported for the third quarter of this year. 

“China’s split economy — booming in tech and slowing in everything else — is coming apart,” says economic analyst Andrew Collier.

Second, domestic investors realize that Xi is trying to take away almost all of the benefits of the country’s tech wonders. For instance, he is commoditizing China’s tech products so that they flood the world. This process, however, reduces corporate profits and therefore investor interest. 

Take the initial public offering of CXMT on July 27. The memory chip firm became the most valuable Chinese public company on its first day of trading. But as Alicia Garcia-Herrero of The Wire China wrote, investors viewed the company as just “another heavily subsidized entrant” that “would now be racing to add capacity into a market already braced for a price war.”  

Investors know by now that they do not control company decisions; Xi does. And he has very different goals than they have. It does not help, as Collier noted, that the “Nvidia blow-up” and related concerns “have scared away some investors in the artificial intelligence boom.”

Because of these fundamental problems, the Chinese government’s support measures have not been particularly effective this year. China’s officials every so often mount a rescue operation by the so-called “national team,” as they did in the middle of July when state-controlled firms went into the market to buy $8.9 billion of shares. But investors this year have been ignoring the government’s desire that they buy stocks.

Earlier this month, the government banned initial public offerings and large stock sales. As the Wall Street Journal’s Lingling Wei wrote, “Intervention looks more like a Band-Aid than a cure.” 

Nothing seems to be working to keep stock prices high, and nothing will work until Xi stops trying to command the economy and the markets.

Gordon G. Chang is the author of “Plan Red: China’s Project to Destroy America” and “The Coming Collapse of China.”

data.title: Boyle says Fetterman 'would probably finish last' in a 2028 Democratic primary
data.description:
Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) said Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) would likely “finish last” in the Democratic primary if he runs for reelection in 2028.

“I think this coffee table could beat John Fetterman in the Democratic primary,” Boyle told Punchbowl News. “If he were to run and it was a five, six-way race, he would probably finish last.”

Fetterman recently hinted at running for reelection in 2028, saying he is “considering things.”

When asked if he is worried about a primary challenger in 2028, Fetterman pointed to Boyle.

“You have the little guy from Philly. You can ask him why he chickened out,” he said.

The House Democrat said he does not plan to challenge Fetterman, instead choosing to remain in the lower chamber where he is in line to be the next chair of the House Budget Committee.

Fetterman recently suggested that could leave the party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is elected as the Senate majority leader, calling it troubling if his “caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being” hostile to Israel. A poll earlier in August showed Fetterman was more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans than Democrats. 

As Fetterman is considering a reelection bid in 2028, multiple candidates are lining up to possibly challenge him for his Senate seat.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said he is seriously considering a 2028 primary challenge against the incumbent, saying, “Fetterman’s been a mess and he doesn’t take the job seriously. Whatever I decide to do, that guy is not going to be the senator in ’28.”

Less than a week after the midterm elections, Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American writer, businessperson and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced a Senate bid against Fetterman.

“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor wrote on the social platform X.

A day after Moor’s announcement, Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) also said she is considering challenging Fetterman, saying, “I have been concerned about, really, two things, which is his family and his health … and am very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes.”

data.title: Zinke says Republicans 'moving on' from Trump
data.description:
GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke (Mont.) on Thursday evening indicated that Republican lawmakers are distancing themselves from President Trump after they lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. 

“They’re moving on, but no doubt, the president took a little pain off them,” Zinke told host Blake Burman on NewsNation’s “The Hill.” “And I would say, some of the damage was below the waterline … but Donald Trump is still a force of nature.”

Democrats are set to regain the majority in both legislative chambers in January, forcing Trump into a “lame duck” presidency for the rest of his term. He will now have to work with Democratic leaders to push his administration’s agenda. 

Zinke, the former Interior secretary under the first Trump administration, announced his retirement from Congress earlier this year, citing ongoing medical procedures. 

The GOP lawmaker emphasized his belief that Trump’s “policies are correct.”

“For instance, the [Iran] war — although unpopular — I agree with 100 percent,” he told Burman, adding, “We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” 

He acknowledged that any failure related to this conflict was tied to the timeline “expectations” set by the president and his administration. 

In March, Trump predicted the conflict, which began in late February, would wrap up in under two months. The ongoing U.S. military operations against Tehran have now stretched over eight months. 

“It wasn’t a 40-hour war. It wasn’t a 72-hour war. It wasn’t a month war,” he said. “But they cannot have a nuclear weapon, otherwise it’ll be in New York and it’ll be here.” 

Zinke also expressed concern during his Thursday interview with NewsNation about the rising national debt, which surpassed the $40 trillion mark in August. 

The outgoing Republican lawmaker accused Congress of “punting” this issue. 

“This is going to come due, and this is why Congress needs to get serious about it,” he said. “Is it a failure? It’s a failure to recognize that affordability is also interest rates, and interest rates are on the basis of how much faith is in the United States government and how much of a budget deficit you’re running.”

data.title: Johnson urges GOP members to show up and vote
data.description:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Friday urged House Republicans to show up and work after GOP leaders had to postpone a procedural rule vote earlier this week over absences.

Johnson wrote in a letter posted to the social platform X that every House Republican needs to “remain fully engaged” over the next 44 days so more GOP priorities can get signed into law. 

“Last night, the Senate passed its permitting reform bill, and we are continuing to work with our colleagues in the other chamber on significant pieces of legislation, including but not limited to government funding and the [National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)]. Beyond that, my aim is to pass in the House every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes, and to put the far-left House Democrats on record to expose their radical ideology,” Johnson wrote.

“To do all of this, we must have full attendance and the support of our entire conference…To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term,” he added.

Fourteen Republicans didn’t show up to vote for a bill the chamber was considering under a fast-track process, known as suspension of the rules, on Wednesday. That number of absences rose to 21 on Thursday.

Johnson told reporters on Thursday that that “attendance is a great frustration for me right now.”

“We’ll be addressing that with members,” he said. 

Lawmakers have just three weeks remaining in the legislative calendar, with Republicans still in control before Democrats assume the majority in January.

Before the transition, Republicans face a packed agenda that includes passing spending legislation ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline to avert a government shutdown and completing work on the annual NDAA.

data.title: The economy is doing better than you think — just not for everyone
data.description:
2026 is almost over, and as we head into the new year, with a new Congress, many are wondering what’s ahead for the U.S. economy.  

Barring any catastrophic events — an AI or crypto bust, a terror attack, more war in the Middle East or elsewhere — so far, so good. In fact, the U.S. economy, and the small businesses that employ half of our workers and make up almost half of our GDP, seem to be doing just fine.  

Then again, it depends on who you ask. 

On the downside, producer prices are up, with increases running more than 6 percent over the past year. That doesn’t bode well for inflation in the months ahead. Higher sustained inflation means not only higher costs, but potentially higher Treasury yields and higher-than-average mortgage rates, which have contributed to the big fall in existing home sales. People in the real estate sector are hurting. 

Speaking of interest, the U.S. Federal Reserve is likely to raise interest rates again before the end of the year, which will make the cost of borrowing higher (the prime rate for business loans is now at 7 percent). The New York Federal Reserve reports that household debt is historically high, and approximately 5 percent of outstanding household debt was delinquent, up from 4.7 percent in the preceding quarter. Approximately 135,000 consumers had new bankruptcy notations added to their credit reports, according to the same report. 

However, inflation excluding gas has cooled a bit, oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and prices at the pump have fallen below $4 on average for the first time since July. Credit card debt also reached record levels, but the rate at which balances transition into serious delinquency improved slightly. This gives consumers more ability to spend. 

And what about those consumers? They drive everything, and they’re not slowing down.  

Retail sales continue to increase. Target says more shoppers are visiting their stores ahead of the holiday season. The National Retail Association is predicting a 4.2 percent growth in holiday sales over last year. Visa is expecting a record increase in holiday spending at retailers. Adobe is saying that consumers will spend 6.7 percent more online than the previous holiday season. That’s great news for merchants. 

There’s also good news for small businesses. American Express, which started Small Business Saturday, says that the annual shopping day after Black Friday will be another success, with 88 percent of consumers they surveyed saying they are likely to shop at small businesses this holiday season — the highest percentage since 2012. 

Small businesses, overall, appear to be weathering the challenges of higher costs, tariffs and a tight job market. Many are uncertain about what’s ahead but, according to one survey from payroll and HR provider Gusto, 86 percent of small-business owners say their companies are meeting or exceeding their original expectations and that they are confident in their own abilities to grow and profit. The National Federation of Business’s closely watched Small Business Optimism Index declined slightly last month, just below its historical average, but its Uncertainty Index fell even more. 

The Institute for Supply Management reports that economic activity in the manufacturing sector expanded in October for the 10th consecutive month. The services sector also continued its record expansion in October, which, according to the ISM, marks the 28th consecutive month in expansion territory. Orders for durable goods also jumped higher than anticipated. 

The job picture still looks pretty good, too. HR firm Paychex says that small employers are showing “resilience” and continuing to add jobs (although hourly rates are still lagging inflation). ADP reports that private-sector employees added 86,000 new jobs just in October, and that overall gross pay increased 4.7 percent year over year. Unemployment claims remain at historically low levels. 

So what does this all mean?  

It means that the U.S. economy is doing well. But that doesn’t mean it’s doing well for everyone. That’s because it never does well for everyone. There are hundreds of millions of people in this country and more than 30 million small businesses. How they’re faring depends on things like we’re they’re located, what industry they’re in, how the weather is and whether or not their business or livelihood is exposed to factors — tariffs, oil prices, etc. — that are out of their control. 

When you hear that the U.S. economy is good, bad, strong or weak, always remember that it depends on where the data is coming from and who you’re asking. So how’s the economy? Seems pretty good to me. But then again, that depends. 

Gene Marks is founder of the Marks Group, a small-business consulting firm.

data.title: Justice Department clears NextEra-Dominion merger
data.description:
The Justice Department (DOJ) on Thursday greenlit the merger between energy companies NextEra and Dominion, after noting concerns about the deal’s impact on electricity costs.

The DOJ said in a release the Internal Market Monitor of ISO New England, who oversees that region’s electric power system, submitted comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) — tasked with approving the NextEra-Dominion merger.

Those comments, the DOJ noted, warned the deal “might give the merged firm the incentive and ability to deactivate” an electricity plant that is “still economically viable.”

The combined entity would do so to “increase capacity payments” in the New England region, the Internal Market Monitor claimed.

Dominion and NextEra announced the nearly $67 billion merger in May, in a deal the two companies said would create the world’s largest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization. The companies said in May they anticipated closing in 12 to 18 months.

To alleviate the Internal Market Monitor’s concerns to FERC, the companies granted the regulator the authority to investigate “any plant that the merged firm proposes to deactivate” for five years starting in May 2028, the DOJ stated. 

Under the agreement, the Internal Market Monitor could bar Florida-based NextEra from deactivating a plant it determines to still have “economic value.”

Given that, the DOJ’s Antitrust Division closed its probe into the merger. The Federal Trade Commission can also raise antitrust concerns about mergers.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) in October called for the combined NextEra-Dominion entity to halt electricity rate hikes for six years if the deal goes through. Dominion is headquartered in Richmond, Va.

The Virginia State Corporation Commission must also approve the merger before the two sides can complete. Opening arguments in the state regulator’s legal review of the deal took place on Tuesday.

Rising utility bills posed a political issue for the GOP this midterm cycle, as Democrats swept to clinch control of Congress and nabbed a majority of governor’s mansions for the first time in 16 years.

Electricity prices increased by by 0.9 percent from September to October, the highest monthly increase since April, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.

data.title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
data.description:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.

And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.

The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years “knowing the love of the father.” Then he told the warden: “Go, warden!”

Almost immediately he exclaimed: “The pain! Go! Go!” He uttered an expletive and implored “the father” to “take this pain.” “Let me go, father,” he said again and again. “Let me go. … I’m here. I’ve been your son all these years.”

Then he shouted: “My right leg is killing me!” and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, “I don’t think this is normal. Take me, father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes’ left foot and on the left side of his neck.

She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state’s procedures.

Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.

Asked if he was faking, she replied, “I think, yeah, there were allegations. … There was nothing abnormal on our part.”

“This isn’t the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It’s also not the first time we’ve had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately,” Hernandez said.

Witness Janice Copeland’s husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.

“David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right,” she said Thursday. “Finally after 30 years, justice has been served.”

Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying, “I never killed anyone.”

Florida has now carried out more than half the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.

Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

Florida husband and wife were strangled

In Florida, Overton was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.

“I’ve never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone,” Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors’ home or gated community. “I didn’t kill the MacIvors.”

The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared him dead.

The MacIvors’ bodies were found in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state’s database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors’ home.

Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.

Michael MacIvor’s sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man’s sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.

“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”

Diamonds missing in jeweler’s killing were never recovered

Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting.

Records showed she also distracted the security guard, David Copeland, at Dennes’ request. Copeland, who was shot twice, identified Dennes as his assailant.

Police found the jeweler’s body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.

Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.

A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.
